\chapter{Hola and Buenos Días}
\label{ch:first-words}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Spanish, say how I am, and wish them a good day.}

A short doorway greeting: hola, an answer to how you are, and buenos días on the way in.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hola]{hola — hello}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-hola}



\begin{quote}
The very first word, and the easiest to say — but there's already one trap hiding in it, and one small mystery.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — the \textbf{h is silent}. \emph{hola} is said \emph{OH-la}, never \emph{HOH-la}. The letter is written but makes no sound at all. This is true of every Spanish \emph{h} you'll ever meet. $\to$ pronunciation reference
  \item \texttt{vowel-o}, \texttt{vowel-a} — two pure vowels: \emph{OH}, \emph{AH}. No glide, no drift.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hola} — hello / hi.

This one is a genuine mystery, and honesty matters more than a tidy story: \emph{hola}'s origin is \textbf{not settled}. It's an old interjection — a hailing call — and that's about as far as the evidence firmly goes. You'll see it confidently linked to English \emph{hello}, or to Arabic \emph{wallāh} (\textquotedblleft{}by God\textquotedblright{}), or to a nautical shout. Treat all of those as \textbf{folk etymology}: plausible- sounding, not established.

In particular, the resemblance to English \emph{hello} is a \textbf{false friend}. English \emph{hello} comes from a Germanic hailing root (\emph{hail}, \emph{holler}, \emph{hollo}) — a completely different family from anything Spanish. The two words sound alike by pure coincidence, not shared ancestry.

\begin{quote}
Why flag this so hard? Because the whole method of this book is building on real family resemblances between Spanish and English. A \emph{fake} one is worse than none — it teaches a connection your brain then has to unlearn. So: enjoy \emph{hola}, but don't file it next to \emph{hello} in your head. They're strangers who happen to look alike.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{hola} is \textbf{informal}. It's the \textquotedblleft{}hi\textquotedblright{} you'd say to a friend, a kid, a shopkeeper you know. It carries no time of day and no deference — which is exactly why, in more formal or first-meeting situations, Spanish speakers reach past it for \emph{buenos días} and its siblings (the next lessons). Knowing \emph{when not} to use \emph{hola} is as much the lesson as the word itself.

Note the written form: an exclamation gets an \textbf{upside-down mark} at the front — \emph{¡hola!} — so you know the tone before you start reading it aloud.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hola\textquotedblright{} — \emph{OH-la}, silent h
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¡hola!\textquotedblright{} to an imagined friend — light, informal
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two things to lock in: what sound does the \emph{h} make? (None.) And is \emph{hola} actually related to English \emph{hello}? (No — a coincidence, a false friend.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hola]{\emph{hola} — let your eye and your hand meet the word}

\label{lesson:ES-W00-hola-observe}



\begin{quote}
Say the greeting you already know: \emph{hola}, \emph{OH-la}. Today adds no new Spanish at all. You will only look at how that one familiar word sits on a page, and let your hand follow it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — one written word}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{h o l a} $\to$ \textbf{hola}
\end{quote}

Count them: \textbf{four} written letters.

Now count what your mouth does: \emph{OH-la} — \textbf{three} sounds.

The extra letter is the one at the front. You met it in the very first lesson: the \textbf{h} is written and says nothing. Here is the same fact seen from the other side — when you \emph{listen}, the \textbf{h} is missing; when you \emph{write}, it must be there.

Point to each letter from left to right, once: \textbf{h}, \textbf{o}, \textbf{l}, \textbf{a}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing — trace with the model visible}
Keep \textbf{hola} visible in front of you the whole time.

Slowly finger-trace the four letters once, left to right. Then trace the word once more in the air.

Say \emph{OH-la} only after your finger has passed the silent \textbf{h} and reached the final \textbf{a}.

This is noticing, not a handwriting test. Use the letter shapes you already write. There is no new alphabet here — Spanish uses the letters you have written all your life.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Touch the silent letter. Stop here — copying comes in the next tiny lesson.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hola]{\emph{hola} — one supported copy}

\label{lesson:ES-W00-hola-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to the first letter in \textbf{hola}. It is written \textbf{h} and it is said as silence.

Keep the model on the page for the whole of this lesson. You are not being asked to remember anything today.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{hola} once. You may look back at the model after every single letter — that is what \textquotedblleft{}guided\textquotedblright{} means here.

When you finish, touch your own \textbf{h-o-l-a} and say \emph{OH-la}.

Your eye checks four letters. Your voice makes three sounds. The hand writes one letter the mouth never says.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Compare only the order of the four letters and whether the \textbf{h} is there. Repair one letter if you need to, then stop. The model stays visible today.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hola]{\emph{hola} — look, hide, write, compare}

\label{lesson:ES-W00-hola-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Look at \textbf{hola} for five seconds. Touch the silent \textbf{h} at the front. Do not copy it yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
1. cover \textbf{hola} 2. wait five seconds 3. write the word once from memory 4. uncover the model and compare \textbf{h-o-l-a}

The place to check first is the front of the word. When the model disappears, the letter your voice never says is the one most likely to go with it.

If one letter differs, circle that place and repair only that letter. A repair is part of the exercise, not a failure.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read your repaired word aloud as \emph{OH-la}. Stop after one memory attempt.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hola]{One heard greeting — write what you know}

\label{lesson:ES-W00-hola-dictation}



\begin{quote}
Cover the answer line lower on this page. You will hear one familiar greeting. No new Spanish is hiding in this lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — short dictation}
{[}YOU HEAR: \emph{OH-la}{]}

Write the Spanish greeting from that sound alone.

Three sounds reached your ear. Four letters belong on your page. Your pen has to supply a letter that the sound never gave you — and it goes first.

Now uncover and compare: \textbf{hola}. Check the four letters and the \textbf{h} at the front. Repair one place if you need to.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Writing from sound is the last step of this four-step runway. It is not a DELE task yet; later lessons grow this from one known word to names, numbers, forms, and short practical messages.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bien]{bien — \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} a whole answer in one word}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-bien}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{hola}. Now the word that carries half of everyday small talk: \emph{bien}. It answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you,\textquotedblright{} it agrees to a plan, it stands completely on its own — and it opens a family of English words you already use.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hola — your first word; \emph{bien} is what you say back when someone asks how you are.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ie} — \textbf{ie} is a quick \emph{YEH}: \emph{bien} is said \emph{byen}, one syllable. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{v-b} — the \textbf{b} is soft, halfway to a \emph{v}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bien} — \textquotedblleft{}well.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{bene} (\textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}). That \emph{bene} is the piece hiding in a shelf of English words, every one about something being \emph{good} or \emph{well}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bene}fit — literally \textquotedblleft{}to do \textbf{well}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{bene} + \emph{facere}).
  \item \textbf{bene}volent — \textquotedblleft{}wishing \textbf{well}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{bene} + \emph{volens}).
  \item \textbf{bene}diction — \textquotedblleft{}speaking \textbf{well},\textquotedblright{} a blessing (\emph{bene} + \emph{dicere}).
  \item \textbf{bene}factor, \textbf{bene}ficial, be\textbf{nign}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{bien} is the Spanish member of the \emph{bene-} family you've owned in English your whole life.

\textbf{Using it on its own.} This is the useful part: \emph{bien} is a complete answer.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\emph{¿Cómo estás?}\textquotedblright{} (how are you?) $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Bien.}\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}Well.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}I'm good.\textquotedblright{} Done.
  \item As agreement, when someone suggests something $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Bien.}\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}Okay / fine.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={The adjective sibling: \emph{bueno} / \emph{buena}}]
\emph{bien} is an \textbf{adverb} — it describes \emph{how} something is done (\textquotedblleft{}you speak \emph{well}\textquotedblright{}). When you want the \textbf{adjective} — to describe a \emph{thing} as \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} — Spanish uses \textbf{bueno} (for a masculine word) or \textbf{buena} (for a feminine word). These come from Latin \textbf{bonus} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}), \emph{bene}'s sibling: Latin split the idea of \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} into an adverb (\emph{bene}) and an adjective (\emph{bonus}), and Spanish kept both. The Latin-descended English cousins of \emph{bueno} are \emph{bonus}, \emph{bonanza}, and \emph{bounty}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{English does the exact same split}: \emph{well} (adverb) vs. \emph{good} (adjective) — \textquotedblleft{}you did \emph{well}\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}a \emph{good} job.\textquotedblright{} English's pair happens to be Germanic, not Latin, so \emph{well/good} aren't blood cousins of \emph{bien/bueno} — but the \emph{structure} is identical, and that parallel is your handle: \textbf{bien = well, bueno/buena = good.}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bien\textquotedblright{} as the answer to \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bueno\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}buena\textquotedblright{} — the adjective, masculine then feminine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which is the adverb (\textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}) and which is the adjective (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{})? (\emph{bien} / \emph{bueno}–\emph{buena}.) And name an English \emph{bene-} cousin of \emph{bien}. (benefit, benevolent, benediction…)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el / la]{el and la — \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} and the gender it carries}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-el-la}



\begin{quote}
Before your first noun, meet two of the smallest, most frequent words in Spanish: \emph{el} and \emph{la}. Both mean \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} Your job here is simply to recognize the pair and connect each form to its label.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item bien / bueno — you saw \emph{bueno} change to \emph{buena}; this lesson explains the gender that made it happen.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-e}, \texttt{vowel-a} — two clean vowels: \emph{el} (\emph{ehl}), \emph{la} (\emph{lah}). $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el} — \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (masculine). \textbf{la} — \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (feminine). English has one word, \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}; Spanish makes this two-way distinction.

\textbf{Where they come from.} Both are worn-down Latin \textbf{demonstratives} — words that meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{that one (over there)}\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{ille} (\textquotedblleft{}that one,\textquotedblright{} masculine).
  \item \textbf{la} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{illa} (\textquotedblleft{}that one,\textquotedblright{} feminine).
\end{itemize}

Over centuries the pointing force faded and the initial \emph{i-} dropped: \emph{ille $\to$ el}, \emph{illa $\to$ la}. What began as \textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{} softened into a plain \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} The same \emph{ille/illa} spread across the whole family — French \emph{le/la}, Italian \emph{il/la} — every Romance \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} is eroded Latin \textquotedblleft{}that.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{The twin thread.} Those \emph{same} Latin words, \emph{ille/illa}, also became Spanish \textbf{él} (\textquotedblleft{}he\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{ella} (\textquotedblleft{}she\textquotedblright{}). So the article \emph{el} (\textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}) and the pronoun \emph{él} (\textquotedblleft{}he\textquotedblright{}) are twins from one Latin parent — told apart only by the accent. (English \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} by contrast, is Germanic and \emph{unrelated} — a shared job, not a shared root.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{el} and \emph{la} are \textbf{articles}: little words that mark \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} Keep them apart from their accented relatives \emph{él} and \emph{ella}, the pronouns \textquotedblleft{}he\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}she.\textquotedblright{} The next micro-lesson explains why Spanish needs two article forms.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}la\textquotedblright{} — the two \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}s
  \item which article goes with a masculine noun? with a feminine one?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form is labelled masculine? (\emph{el}.) Which is labelled feminine? (\emph{la}.) Both come from Latin words meaning what? (\textquotedblleft{}That one\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ille} / \emph{illa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el / la + noun]{Grammatical gender — the two noun classes behind \emph{el} and \emph{la}}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-genero-gramatical}



\begin{quote}
You know that \emph{el} and \emph{la} both mean \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} Now give their two labels: \emph{el} is masculine; \emph{la} is feminine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el / la — the two definite articles.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: grammatical gender}]
Every Spanish noun belongs to one of two \textbf{grammatical classes}, traditionally called masculine and feminine. This is not a claim about biological sex. It is a matching system: a masculine noun uses \emph{el}; a feminine noun uses \emph{la}.

Latin had masculine, feminine, and neuter classes. Spanish reduced that three-way system to two, with most old neuter nouns joining the masculine class. The word \emph{gender} itself comes through Latin \emph{genus}, \textquotedblleft{}kind\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}class.\textquotedblright{}

You cannot always predict a noun's class from its ending. Learn each new noun with its article, as one small unit: \emph{el + noun} or \emph{la + noun}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the article for a noun labelled masculine
  \item the article for a noun labelled feminine
  \item what grammatical gender classifies — nouns, not people
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many noun classes did Latin have? (Three.) How many does Spanish keep? (Two.) What should travel with every new noun you learn? (Its article, \emph{el} or \emph{la}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[día]{día — your first noun}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-dia}



\begin{quote}
You just learned how Spanish tags gender with \emph{el} / \emph{la}. Now put it to work on your very first noun — \emph{día}, \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el / la — grammatical gender and the two \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}s; \emph{día} is where you apply them.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{accent-i} — the accent sits on the \textbf{í}: \emph{día} is \emph{DEE-a}, two beats. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{d-soft} — the \textbf{d} between vowels is soft, toward the \emph{th} in \emph{this}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el día} — \textquotedblleft{}the day.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{dies} (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}). The family fans across English, mostly through French:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{di}ary, \textbf{di}urnal (\textquotedblleft{}of the day\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{jour}nal, \textbf{jour}ney — French \emph{jour}, \textquotedblleft{}a day\textquotedblright{} (a \emph{journey} was once \textquotedblleft{}a day's travel\textquotedblright{}).
  \item quoti\textbf{di}an (\textquotedblleft{}every-day\textquotedblright{}), meri\textbf{di}an (\textquotedblleft{}mid-day\textquotedblright{}), and \emph{dismal} (\emph{dies mali}, \textquotedblleft{}evil days\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Its two tags: gender and number}]
You already know gender from the last lesson; here's how \emph{día} wears it.

\textbf{Gender.} \emph{día} is \textbf{masculine} — \emph{el día} — which is a small surprise, because it ends in \emph{-a}, the ending that usually signals feminine. Why the exception? Because Latin \emph{dies} was masculine, and \emph{día} inherited that gender whole, spelling be damned. (This is exactly why gender must be learned \emph{with} the word, not guessed from the ending — and it's the first of several \textquotedblleft{}\emph{-a}-but-masculine\textquotedblright{} nouns you'll meet.)

\textbf{Number.} One rule for now: a noun ending in a vowel adds \textbf{-s}. \emph{día $\to$ días} (\textquotedblleft{}days\textquotedblright{}). (Consonant endings take \emph{-es} — later.)
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why the gender matters next}]
Gender isn't a passive label — it \emph{forces} the words around the noun to match. The very next lesson, \emph{buenos días}, turns \emph{bueno} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) into \emph{buen\textbf{os}} precisely because \emph{día} is masculine and plural. So the gender you just attached to \emph{día} is about to earn its keep.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el día\textquotedblright{} — with its masculine \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}días\textquotedblright{} — plural, vowel + \emph{-s}
  \item is \emph{día} masculine or feminine, and why? (masculine — from Latin \emph{dies}, despite the \emph{-a})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} goes with \emph{día}, and why? (\emph{el} — masculine, inherited from Latin \emph{dies}, despite the \emph{-a} ending.) How do you make it plural? (\emph{días} — vowel + \emph{-s}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[buenos días]{buenos días — the greeting you say before noon}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-buenos-dias}



\begin{quote}
You can already greet someone at any hour with \emph{hola}. Now the one you use in the morning — the greeting everyone knows.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item día — the word \emph{day}, which you have already met.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ue} — \textbf{ue} is a quick \emph{WEH}: \emph{bueno} is \emph{BWEH-no}.
  \item \texttt{accent-i} — \emph{días} keeps its stress on the \emph{í}: \emph{DEE-as}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{buenos días} is, word for word, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}good days\textquotedblright{}} — plural, and nobody knows quite why the plural stuck. Spanish says it in the plural and always has.

Take it whole. It is one thing you say, not two things you assemble: \emph{buenos días}, said as a single run, the way English says \emph{good morning} without stopping to think about \emph{good} or \emph{morning}.

\begin{quote}
The shape of it — why \emph{buenos} and not \emph{bueno} — is a real rule, and a useful one. It is also not the rule you need in order to say hello before lunch. It comes later, once you have enough words for it to be worth explaining.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
So why \textquotedblleft{}good \textbf{days},\textquotedblright{} plural at all? Because \emph{buenos días} is a \textbf{fossil} — the worn-down stub of a blessing: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Buenos días os dé Dios,\textquotedblright{}} \emph{\textquotedblleft{}may God give you good days.\textquotedblright{}} You weren't wishing one good morning; you were asking heaven for many good days ahead. The plural is the last bone of that prayer — and it's why \emph{buenos días} feels warm and a little formal, where \emph{hola} is casual. It is, almost literally, a small \emph{bene}diction (the \emph{bien} lesson's word). \emph{(A widely-accepted account; exact history debated.)}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item build it slowly — \textquotedblleft{}bueno\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}días\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}buenos días\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hola, buenos días\textquotedblright{} — casual + warm, stacked
  \item why is it \emph{buenos}, not \emph{bueno}? (out loud, in your own words)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two things: why is it \emph{buenos} and not \emph{bueno}? (Agreement — \emph{días} is masculine plural.) And what blessing was \emph{buenos días} shortened from? (\textquotedblleft{}May God give you good days.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — hola and buenos días}

\label{lesson:ES-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
End of the chapter. No new words — just the four you have, turned over until they're automatic.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
In four short lessons you went from nothing to two full greetings and the first two rules of Spanish grammar:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hola} — the casual \textquotedblleft{}hi.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{bien} — \textquotedblleft{}well/good,\textquotedblright{} a complete answer on its own; and its adjective sibling \textbf{bueno / buena}.
  \item \textbf{día $\to$ días} — a noun, and the plural rule (vowel + \emph{-s}).
  \item \textbf{buenos días} — assembled from \emph{bueno} + \emph{días}, with \textbf{agreement} turning \emph{bueno} into \emph{buenos} to match.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say each out loud; don't just read.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item greet a friend casually — \emph{hola}
  \item greet someone warmly in the morning — \emph{buenos días}
  \item stack them — \emph{hola, buenos días}
  \item answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{} with one word — \emph{bien}
  \item the four shapes of \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} — \emph{bueno, buena, buenos, buenas} — and for each, is it masculine/feminine, singular/plural?
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Build \emph{buenos días} from scratch, out loud: \emph{bueno} $\to$ agree with masculine-plural \emph{días} $\to$ \emph{buenos días}. Do it until the \textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{} feels obvious, not memorized.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You can now greet two ways and give a one-word positive answer. The very next question is the one that opens a real conversation: when \emph{someone else} says \emph{buenos días} to you — \textbf{what do you say back?} That's the whole next chapter, and it's where these words start turning into an exchange.
\end{tcolorbox}
